title: Financial Accounting

pattern.summary: 9 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. No compulsory question. Roughly half the paper is theory and half is numerical problems.

choosing: Q9 (computerised accounting / Tally) is theory and often lets you pick two of three notes — a reliable choice.
numerical: Draw proper T-accounts or formats with Dr/Cr and dates. Show the balancing figure clearly.
Write working notes for every calculation (interest, loading, closing stock) — they earn marks on their own.

topics.name: Computerised Accounting & Tally
topics.summary: Usually the last question (Q9), always theory, often 'write notes on any two'. The most predictable 20 marks in the paper.
points: Computerised accounting is used for speed, ease, security and reliability; the risks are data corruption, power problems, theft of data and over-reliance on computers.
The key difference from manual accounting: ledgers are created first, and transactions are then entered through vouchers, instead of journal entries followed by ledger posting.
Choose software on factors such as cost, ease of use, flexibility, data security, vendor support and statutory compliance.
Step 1 in Tally ERP.9 is company creation (name, address, contact details, with or without inventory, financial year). Features apply only to that company; configurations apply to the whole software.

Step 2 is creating masters. Tally has 2 predefined ledgers (Cash, and Profit & Loss) and 28 predefined groups — 15 primary (9 for balance sheet items, 6 for profit and loss) and 13 sub-groups. Inventory masters: stock groups, categories, units, godowns and stock items.

Step 3 is recording vouchers: 8 main voucher types (contra, payment, receipt, journal, sales, purchase, credit note, debit note) plus reversing journal, memorandum and post-dated vouchers. Entries can be checked and altered in the Day Book.
Invoices can be raised as an Account Invoice (services) or an Item Invoice (with item details).
Step 4 is reports, produced automatically: Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss, Stock Summary and Trial Balance on the main screen; Day Book, receivables, payables and cash/bank books under Display.
topics.frame: Definition (2–3 lines) → 5–6 headed points with one line each → a small comparison table where relevant → one-line conclusion.
mistakes: Writing only definitions — each 10-mark note needs 5–6 distinct points.
Mixing up stock group and stock category.
examples:
Example: Sharma Traders starts using Tally
Company creation: name, address and the financial year from 1 April, with inventory switched on.
Masters: ledgers such as Sharma Capital (under Capital Account), SBI (under Bank Accounts), Rent (under Indirect Expenses) and Ravi & Co (under Sundry Creditors); stock items with their units.
Vouchers: rent of ₹10,000 paid by cheque → Payment voucher (Rent Dr, SBI Cr). Goods bought on credit from Ravi & Co → Purchase voucher.
Reports: the Trial Balance, Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet appear on their own — nothing is posted or totalled by hand.

Example: which voucher?
Cash deposited into the bank → Contra.
Salary paid in cash → Payment.
Commission received by cheque → Receipt.
Depreciation charged for the year → Journal.
Goods returned by a customer → Credit Note; goods returned to a supplier → Debit Note.

topics.name: Branch Accounts
topics.summary: Either a numerical (Branch Account / Stock & Debtors system) or theory on systems of dependent branches.
points: Branch accounts show each branch's profit or loss and help control its stock and cash.
Dependent branches keep no full books — the head office keeps their accounts. Independent branches keep a full double-entry system and prepare their own trial balance.
Systems for dependent branches: Debtors system (a Branch Account works like a Profit and Loss account), Stock and Debtors system, and Final Accounts system.
When goods are invoiced to the branch above cost, the loading on goods sent, returns, and opening and closing stock is removed so only real profit is shown.
Independent branches: the head office keeps a Branch Account and the branch keeps a Head Office Account; each mirrors the other.

Items needing special treatment: goods in transit, cash in transit, head-office expenses charged to the branch, depreciation on branch assets whose accounts are kept at head office, and inter-branch transactions.

Incorporating the branch trial balance: detailed incorporation (every item) or abridged incorporation (branch profit or loss plus assets and liabilities). The Branch Account then closes and reopens next year.
method: Debtors system: open Branch A/c. Debit: opening stock, opening debtors, petty cash, prepaid expenses, goods sent, cash sent for expenses. Credit: cash remitted by branch (cash sales + collections), goods returned to HO, closing stock, closing debtors, closing petty cash.
Liabilities work the other way: opening outstanding expenses on the credit side, closing outstanding expenses on the debit side.
Credit sales, discounts, bad debts and returns by customers do NOT enter the Branch Account (they are inside the debtors figure).
If goods are sent at invoice price: bring stock and goods sent at invoice price, then remove loading with contra entries (Stock Reserve / Goods sent to Branch).
Balancing figure of Branch A/c = profit (credit shortfall) or loss.
formula: e.g. cost + 25% → loading = 25/125 = 1/5 of invoice price
mistakes: Putting credit sales in the Branch Account under the debtors system.
Forgetting to remove loading on opening and closing stock.
examples:
Example: debtors system, goods invoiced at cost + 25%
Loading = 25 ÷ 125 = 1/5 of the invoice price.
Data (at invoice price): opening stock ₹20,000, goods sent ₹1,00,000, closing stock ₹25,000. Opening debtors ₹10,000, closing debtors ₹15,000. Cash sent for expenses ₹8,000. Branch remitted cash sales ₹40,000 + collections ₹50,000.
Branch A/c debit: opening stock 20,000 + opening debtors 10,000 + goods sent 1,00,000 + cash for expenses 8,000 + stock reserve on closing stock 5,000 = ₹1,43,000.
Branch A/c credit: cash remitted 90,000 + closing stock 25,000 + closing debtors 15,000 + loading on goods sent 20,000 + loading on opening stock 4,000 = ₹1,54,000.
Branch profit = 1,54,000 − 1,43,000 = ₹11,000.

Check the same answer at cost
Cost of goods sold = opening stock 16,000 + goods sent 80,000 − closing stock 20,000 = ₹76,000.
Sales = cash 40,000 + credit sales (15,000 + 50,000 − 10,000 = 55,000) = ₹95,000.
Profit = 95,000 − 76,000 − expenses 8,000 = ₹11,000 — the same, which shows why all the loading had to be removed.

topics.name: Joint Venture
topics.summary: Recently as a full numerical (Memorandum JV + JV with co-venturer's account) and as theory on methods.
points: A joint venture is a temporary partnership of two or more persons for a specific project; it ends automatically when the project is complete.
It differs from a partnership (temporary, one project, no firm name) and from a consignment (co-venturers are co-owners sharing profit, not principal and agent).

The book's four methods: (1) one co-venturer records everything; (2) every co-venturer records all transactions; (3) each records only his own transactions and a Memorandum Joint Venture Account is prepared at the end; (4) separate books for the venture.
Under methods 1 and 2 the Joint Venture Account works as the venture's profit and loss account; under method 3 each keeps a 'Joint Venture with …' personal account instead.
With separate books: Joint Venture Account, Joint Bank Account and the co-venturers' personal accounts — kept strictly on double entry.
method: Memorandum JV Account (= a P&L of the venture): Debit all expenses and goods bought by all venturers; credit sales and stock/assets taken over. Balance = profit, shared in ratio.
'Joint Venture with X Account' in A's books: Debit A's own purchases/expenses and A's share of profit; credit A's own sales and goods A takes over. Balance = amount due to/from X, settled by cash.
Separate books: Joint Bank A/c (contributions in, payments out), JV A/c (all expenses, sales, profit), Co-venturers' A/cs (contribution + profit share − withdrawals).
formula: Profit share = JV profit × agreed ratio
mistakes: Recording the other venturer's transactions in 'JV with X' account under the Memorandum method.
Forgetting stock or plant taken over by a venturer on the credit side.
examples:
Example: A and B, profit shared 3 : 2, each keeps only his own transactions
A buys goods ₹50,000 and pays expenses ₹5,000. B pays carriage ₹3,000, sells all but a little stock for ₹80,000 and takes over the unsold stock at ₹4,000.
Memorandum JV A/c: debit 50,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 = ₹58,000; credit 80,000 + 4,000 = ₹84,000. Profit ₹26,000 → A ₹15,600, B ₹10,400.
In A's books, 'JV with B A/c': debit purchases 50,000 + expenses 5,000 + profit 15,600 = ₹70,600, no credits → B owes A ₹70,600.
Check from B's side: sales 80,000 + stock 4,000 − carriage 3,000 − profit 10,400 = ₹70,600. B pays A this amount to settle.

topics.name: Hire Purchase & Instalment
topics.summary: Theory on features and hirer's accounting, numericals with default and repossession.
points: Under hire purchase the buyer gets possession at once but ownership passes only with the last instalment; on default the seller can take the goods back.
Hire purchase price = cash price + interest; knowing any two gives the third.
The buyer (hirer) records the asset at its full cash price or at the cash price actually paid; the main accounts are the Asset Account and the Hire Vendor Account.
The vendor keeps the Hire Purchaser's Account and an Interest Account.
On default the vendor may repossess all of the goods, or only part by agreement — the repossessed part is revalued and adjusted against the amount due.

Instalment payment system: ownership passes when the contract is signed. The buyer is debited with the total interest at the start through an Interest Suspense Account, released as instalments fall due.
Goods of small value: the vendor keeps a Hire Purchase Sales Register and works out profit by the Debtors method (Hire Purchase Trading Account) or the Stock and Debtors method.
Missing figures in the Hire Purchase Trading Account are found through memorandum accounts: Stock at Shop, Stock with Customers and Instalments Due.
method: Find interest per instalment: interest = rate × outstanding cash price (work backwards when cash price is not given).
Asset A/c Dr (full cash price) To Vendor A/c.
Each instalment: Interest A/c Dr To Vendor A/c; then Vendor A/c Dr To Bank A/c.
Depreciation on full cash price each year; interest and depreciation to P&L.
Default and repossession (hirer): Vendor A/c Dr To Asset A/c (with the amount still due); the rest of the returned goods' book value is a loss on repossession, transferred to P&L.
formula: Interest = Opening balance of cash price × Rate
Total interest = Hire purchase price − Cash price
mistakes: Charging depreciation on the instalments paid instead of full cash price.
Deducting interest from the down payment.
examples:
Example: machine on hire purchase, interest 10% on the balance
Cash price ₹50,000; ₹14,000 down, rest in three yearly instalments with interest.
Year 1: interest 10% × 36,000 = 3,600; instalment 15,600 (12,000 principal). Balance 24,000.
Year 2: interest 2,400; instalment 14,400. Balance 12,000.
Year 3: interest 1,200; instalment 13,200. Balance nil.
Hire purchase price = 14,000 + 15,600 + 14,400 + 13,200 = ₹57,200; total interest = 57,200 − 50,000 = ₹7,200.
Hirer's entries: Machinery A/c Dr 50,000 To Vendor A/c. Each year: Interest A/c Dr To Vendor A/c, then Vendor A/c Dr To Bank A/c. Depreciation is on the full ₹50,000.

Example: default and repossession (same machine)
The hirer cannot pay the third instalment and the vendor takes the machine back. Depreciation at 10% a year on cost for 2 years = ₹10,000, so book value = ₹40,000.
Amount due to the vendor = balance 12,000 + year-3 interest 1,200 = ₹13,200 (Interest A/c Dr To Vendor A/c 1,200 first).
Vendor A/c Dr 13,200 To Machinery A/c. The rest of the book value, 40,000 − 13,200 = ₹26,800, is the loss on repossession, transferred to Profit and Loss.

topics.name: Consignment
topics.summary: Numericals on Consignment Account and valuation of unsold stock, theory on invoice price, loading and losses.
points: In a consignment, the consignor (owner) sends goods to a consignee (agent) who sells them for a commission. Their relationship is that of principal and agent.
A proforma invoice goes with the goods; after selling, the consignee sends an account sales showing units sold, prices, expenses, commission and the balance due.
Commission may be ordinary or special; del credere commission is paid when the consignee bears the risk of bad debts.
The consignor's accounts: Consignment Account, Goods Sent on Consignment Account and the Consignee's Account. The consignee's: Commission Account and the Consignor's Account.
Unsold stock is valued at cost plus a proportion of non-recurring expenses; selling expenses are not added.

Normal loss is not recorded separately — it raises the cost per unit of the remaining goods. Abnormal loss is valued like unsold stock, credited to the Consignment Account, and charged to Profit and Loss after deducting any insurance claim.

Invoice price (IP) is set above cost to hide the profit; loading = IP − cost price. Loading affects four items — goods sent, goods returned, opening stock and closing stock — and is removed by adjusting entries in the consignor's books only.
method: Consignment A/c (Dr): goods sent, consignor's expenses, consignee's expenses, commission. (Cr): sales, abnormal loss, closing stock. Balance = profit/loss.
Unsold stock value = (Cost of goods + consignor's expenses + consignee's non-recurring expenses) × unsold units ÷ units received.
Consignee's selling expenses (godown rent, selling) are NOT added to stock value.
Commission: ordinary on total sales; over-riding on surplus above invoice; del credere on total credit sales.
formula: Closing stock = (Total cost incl. direct expenses) ÷ Units received × Units unsold
Normal loss: units received = sent − normal loss
mistakes: Adding selling expenses to closing stock.
Treating normal loss as abnormal loss.
examples:
Example: consignment with unsold stock
A of Delhi sends 100 units costing ₹500 each (₹50,000) to B of Mumbai and pays freight ₹2,000. B pays unloading ₹1,000 (non-recurring) and godown rent ₹1,500 (selling), sells 80 units at ₹800 and gets 5% commission.
Closing stock (20 units) = (50,000 + 2,000 + 1,000) × 20 ÷ 100 = ₹10,600 — godown rent is not added.
Consignment A/c debit: goods 50,000 + A's freight 2,000 + B's expenses 2,500 + commission 3,200 = ₹57,700. Credit: sales 64,000 + stock 10,600 = ₹74,600. Profit ₹16,900.
B owes A: sales 64,000 − expenses 2,500 − commission 3,200 = ₹58,300.

Example: normal loss raises the cost per unit
1,000 kg sent at ₹20 per kg with freight ₹2,000 (total ₹22,000). Normal loss in transit 50 kg, so 950 kg arrive; 760 kg are sold.
Closing stock = 22,000 ÷ 950 × 190 kg = ₹4,400. The 50 kg loss is not shown separately — its cost is spread over the good units.

topics.name: Trial Balance, Errors & Rectification
topics.summary: Usually a 20-mark rectification with Suspense Account.
points: A trial balance lists ledger balances to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books and to provide a summary for final accounts.
It may disagree because of errors such as wrong totals, wrong posting, posting to the wrong side, omitting one side, or wrong balancing.

Errors not disclosed by a trial balance: errors of principle (e.g. a machine bought on credit entered in the Purchases Journal — capital treated as revenue), complete omission, errors of commission posted to the wrong account of the same class, and compensating errors.
Advantages: checks arithmetical accuracy, helps locate errors, summarises balances for final accounts. Limitation: agreement does not prove the books are error-free.
Rectification: find what was done and what should have been done, then pass the correcting entry.
One-sided errors found after the trial balance is drawn go through a Suspense Account, which must close to nil once all errors are corrected.
Rectifying entries that involve nominal accounts change the profit already calculated.
method: For each error, write what was done, what should have been done, then the correcting entry.
If the error affects only one account (e.g. wrong posting, casting error), use Suspense A/c for the other side.
If both sides are wrong (e.g. entered in wrong book), no suspense — correct both accounts.
Post all suspense entries to Suspense A/c; it must close to zero.
formula: Undercasting of Sales Book → Suspense A/c Dr To Sales A/c
Overcasting of Purchase Book → Suspense A/c Dr To Purchases A/c
mistakes: Using suspense for errors that don't affect the trial balance.
Reversing the sign of casting errors.
examples:
Example: rectification with a suspense account
The trial balance debit total is ₹750 more than the credit total, so Suspense A/c is opened with a credit of ₹750. Errors found later:
(a) Sales Book undercast by ₹1,000 → Suspense A/c Dr 1,000 To Sales A/c 1,000.
(b) Furniture ₹5,000 bought was debited to Purchases (error of principle — both sides exist, so no suspense) → Furniture A/c Dr 5,000 To Purchases A/c 5,000.
(c) Discount allowed ₹250 not posted to Discount A/c → Discount Allowed A/c Dr 250 To Suspense A/c 250.
Suspense A/c: debit 1,000; credit 750 + 250 = 1,000 → closes to nil.
Effect on profit: +1,000 (sales) + 5,000 (purchases lower) − 250 (discount) = ₹5,750 more profit.

topics.name: Depreciation
topics.summary: Mostly a 20-mark theory question on meaning and methods; sometimes a Machinery Account numerical.
points: Depreciation is a permanent, gradual fall in the value of a fixed asset through use and passage of time; it is the expired cost charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
Without it, profit is overstated and the balance sheet does not show the true financial position.
Related terms: depletion (wasting assets such as mines), amortisation (intangible assets), obsolescence (becoming out of date).
The amount depends on the asset's cost, estimated useful life and estimated salvage (scrap) value.

Two ways of recording: credit depreciation directly to the Asset Account each year, or credit a Provision for Depreciation Account (transferred to the asset when it is sold or retired). The balance sheet shows the asset at depreciated value either way.
The book's eight methods: fixed instalment, diminishing balance, annuity, depreciation fund, insurance policy, revaluation, depletion and machine hour rate. The first two are the most common.

Fixed instalment charges the same amount each year; diminishing balance charges less each year. The book prefers diminishing balance because depreciation plus repairs stays roughly even over the asset's life.
A change of method with retrospective effect needs depreciation worked out both ways and the difference adjusted.
method: Machinery A/c: purchase cost + installation; depreciation each year (pro rata for part years).
On sale: find book value on date of sale; profit/loss = sale price − book value; transfer to P&L.
mistakes: Not charging depreciation for the part year before sale.
Leaving out installation charges from cost.
examples:
Example: the two common methods
Machine bought on 1 April for ₹90,000 plus installation ₹10,000 = cost ₹1,00,000. Scrap value ₹10,000, life 5 years.
Fixed instalment: (1,00,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = ₹18,000 every year.
Diminishing balance at 20%: year 1 ₹20,000, year 2 ₹16,000 (20% of 80,000), year 3 ₹12,800 (20% of 64,000) — less each year.
Part year: had it been bought on 1 October, the first year's charge would be for 6 months only (₹9,000 under fixed instalment).

Example: sale of the machine (fixed instalment)
Sold after 2 full years for ₹70,000. Book value = 1,00,000 − 2 × 18,000 = ₹64,000.
Profit on sale = 70,000 − 64,000 = ₹6,000, transferred to Profit and Loss.

topics.name: Accounting Concepts, Conventions & Income
points: Concepts (generally accepted accounting principles) are ground rules for recording and reporting; some apply at the recording stage, others at the reporting stage.

Recording stage: business entity (business and owner are separate), money measurement (record in the country's currency), historical record (record only what has happened, date-wise), cost (record the amount paid, not the value) and dual aspect (every transaction has two sides).
Reporting stage: going concern (the firm continues, it is not closing down), accounting period, matching (match costs with the revenues of the same period), accrual and realisation.
Conservatism (prudence): provide for all losses but take only incomes actually earned.
Consistency: follow the same methods from period to period so figures can be compared.
Full disclosure: reports must disclose all material information users need.
Materiality: facts that are not material may be ignored when measuring income.
Measuring business income relies on the accounting period, realisation (revenue recognition), matching and accrual.
topics.frame: One-line meaning of each concept + one example each. For 20 marks, cover 8–10 concepts with examples.
mistakes: Listing names without examples.
examples:
Examples: which concept applies?
The owner takes ₹5,000 from the business till for household use → recorded as drawings, because the business is separate from its owner (business entity).
Land bought for ₹10 lakh is now worth ₹15 lakh → it stays at ₹10 lakh in the books (cost).
Closing stock cost ₹50,000 but can now be sold for only ₹45,000 → shown at ₹45,000; an expected profit is not recorded (conservatism).
March salary paid on 5 April → an expense of the year ending 31 March (accrual and matching).
A ₹150 stapler is written off as an expense rather than depreciated (materiality).
The firm keeps using the same stock valuation method every year (consistency).

topics.name: Accounting Process & Double Entry
topics.summary: Mostly 10-mark theory: double entry, rules of debit and credit, process, bases of accounting.
points: Accounting process: record in the journal → post to the ledger → prepare a trial balance → prepare final accounts → analyse and report.
Accounts are personal (dealings with persons), real (assets) or nominal (expenses, losses, incomes and gains).
Every transaction has a receiving and a giving aspect; recording both is double entry — for every debit there is an equal credit.
Rules — personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver; real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out; nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.
Advantages of double entry: complete record, arithmetical check through the trial balance, profit and financial position can be found, fraud is easier to detect.
Single entry is an incomplete record of transactions; double entry is the complete system.
Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
topics.frame: Definition → features/advantages as headed points → a small example entry or table.
examples:
Example: the accounting equation, one step at a time
Ramesh starts with cash ₹1,00,000 → Assets 1,00,000 = Capital 1,00,000.
Buys goods on credit from Gopal ₹30,000 → Assets 1,30,000 = Liabilities 30,000 + Capital 1,00,000.
Sells goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹15,000 cash → cash 1,15,000 + stock 20,000 = 1,35,000 = 30,000 + capital 1,05,000 (profit adds to capital).
Pays rent ₹2,000 → Assets 1,33,000 = 30,000 + 1,03,000. Both sides stay equal every time.

Examples: applying the rules
Rent paid in cash → Rent A/c Dr (nominal: expense) To Cash A/c (real: goes out).
Goods sold to Sita on credit → Sita A/c Dr (personal: receiver) To Sales A/c.
Commission received by cheque → Bank A/c Dr (real: comes in) To Commission A/c (nominal: income).

topics.name: Nature, Scope & Users of Accounting
points: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating financial transactions and events.
Need: a business has too many transactions to remember, and both insiders and outsiders need systematic information about it.
Objectives: keep systematic records, find the profit or loss, show the financial position, and give information to interested parties for decisions.
Book-keeping is the record-keeping part of accounting and stops at classifying; accounting goes on to summarise, analyse and report. Accountancy is the body of knowledge; accounting is its practice.
Users: owners, management, lenders, creditors, investors, tax authorities, employees, customers and the public — each wants different information.
Branches: financial, cost and management accounting grew as business and management became more complex.
Qualitative characteristics of accounting information: understandability, relevance, reliability and comparability.
Bases of accounting: cash basis (record only when cash is received or paid) and accrual basis (record when earned or incurred) — the book calls accrual the more rational basis.
Limitations: records only money-measurable events, uses historical cost, involves estimates and personal judgement.
topics.frame: Definition → objectives or users as headed points (one line each, what each user wants) → conclusion.
examples:
Example: what each user looks for in a shop's accounts
The owner: profit for the year. A bank asked for a loan: can the business pay interest and repay? A supplier: will its bills be paid on time? The tax department: taxable income. Employees: can the business pay salaries and bonus?

Example: cash basis vs accrual basis
Goods worth ₹20,000 are sold on credit in March and the money comes in April. Accrual basis records the sale in March, when it was earned; cash basis records it only in April, when cash is received — so March profit looks lower on a cash basis.

topics.name: Accounting Standards (AS, Ind AS, IFRS)
topics.summary: Mostly 10-mark theory: objectives, procedure in India, Ind AS vs IFRS.
points: Accounting standards are written statements of accounting rules and guidelines for preparing uniform and consistent financial statements.
Objectives: provide information, harmonise different accounting practices, and bring uniformity, consistency and comparability.
Benefits: true and fair view, easy comparison, more valuable information, efficient management, help to accountants and auditors, more credibility and reliability.

In India the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of ICAI frames standards: ASB (with a study group) → exposure draft circulated for comments → ASB revises and submits to the ICAI Council → ICAI issues the standard.
Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires companies to follow the prevailing standards; as on 1 April 2016 there were 32 accounting standards.
IFRS: a single global set of standards developed by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB); used across borders to make statements comparable.
India converged its standards with IFRS; the converged standards are called Ind AS. Ind AS 101 covers first-time adoption (moving from Indian GAAP to Ind AS).
topics.frame: Definition → objectives → steps as a numbered list → comparison table where asked.
examples:
Example: why a standard is needed
Two shops buy the same goods at rising prices. One values closing stock by FIFO, the other by a weighted average, so their profits differ even though their business is the same. A standard on inventories (AS 2) sets common rules, so the figures can be compared.

Example: moving to Ind AS
Indian companies above set size limits (the first phase covered companies with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, from 1 April 2016) had to prepare accounts under Ind AS, which are converged with IFRS. The first year's switch from old Indian GAAP is handled under Ind AS 101.

topics.name: Final Accounts
topics.summary: Trading & P&L / Balance Sheet numericals and format questions.
points: Final accounts are the Profit and Loss Account (with a Trading section) and the Balance Sheet, prepared from the trial balance at the year end.
Trading Account shows gross profit: sales minus cost of goods sold, including direct expenses.
Profit and Loss Account shows net profit: gross profit and other incomes minus indirect expenses and losses. Closing entries transfer expenses and incomes to these accounts.

Balance Sheet: assets are the debit balances of real and personal accounts (plus deferred revenue expenses not yet written off); liabilities are the credit balances, including capital. The two totals are always equal.
Assets may be arranged in order of liquidity or permanence; companies use a vertical presentation.
A Manufacturing Account (optional) finds the cost of goods produced, which is carried to the Trading Account.
method: Classify each item: direct (Trading) vs indirect (P&L) vs balance sheet.
Carriage inwards/wages → Trading; carriage on sales, salaries, rent → P&L.
Apply adjustments before totalling.
formula: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Purchase returns + Direct expenses − Closing stock
mistakes: Putting carriage on sales in Trading A/c.
Forgetting closing stock on both P&L side (Trading credit) and Balance Sheet.
examples:
Example: from trial balance to net profit
Opening stock ₹20,000, purchases ₹1,00,000, purchase returns ₹5,000, wages ₹10,000, carriage inwards ₹3,000, closing stock ₹25,000. Sales ₹1,60,000, sales returns ₹4,000.
Cost of goods sold = 20,000 + 1,00,000 − 5,000 + 10,000 + 3,000 − 25,000 = ₹1,03,000.
Gross profit = net sales 1,56,000 − 1,03,000 = ₹53,000 (Trading section).
Indirect items: salaries ₹15,000, rent ₹6,000, carriage outwards ₹2,000; commission received ₹1,000.
Net profit = 53,000 + 1,000 − 23,000 = ₹31,000, added to capital in the Balance Sheet.

topics.name: Adjustments in Final Accounts
topics.summary: 20-mark theory question on the adjustments and their two-fold effect.
points: Adjustments are needed because some expenses and incomes relate to more than one year or are still outstanding; without them the accounts do not show a true picture.
An adjustment given outside the trial balance appears at two places in the final accounts, completing the double entry; one already inside an adjusted trial balance appears only once.
Closing stock: credit side of the Trading Account and an asset in the Balance Sheet.
Outstanding expenses: added to the expense and shown as a liability. Prepaid expenses: deducted from the expense and shown as an asset.
Accrued income: added to the income and shown as an asset. Income received in advance: deducted from the income and shown as a liability.
Depreciation, bad debts and provision for doubtful debts: debited to Profit and Loss and deducted from the asset or debtors.
Interest on capital is an expense of the business; interest on drawings is an income.
topics.frame: Meaning of adjustment → each adjustment with its two effects (P&L side and Balance Sheet) — a table works well.
mistakes: Showing only one effect of an adjustment (every adjustment has two).
examples:
Examples: each adjustment appears twice
Rent paid ₹11,000 for 11 months; one month (₹1,000) is outstanding → P&L rent ₹12,000; ₹1,000 shown as a liability.
Insurance ₹12,000 paid on 1 October for one year; books close on 31 March → ₹6,000 is prepaid: P&L ₹6,000; prepaid ₹6,000 shown as an asset.
Debtors ₹50,000; write off further bad debts ₹2,000 and make a 5% provision (no old provision) → provision = 5% of 48,000 = ₹2,400; P&L is charged 2,000 + 2,400; debtors shown at 50,000 − 2,000 − 2,400 = ₹45,600.
Interest on capital ₹3,000 → debited to P&L and added to capital.

topics.name: Subsidiary Books (Cash Book, Purchase Book)
topics.summary: Cash book / purchases book numericals and 'why is the journal sub-divided'.
points: The journal is sub-divided when repetitive transactions are numerous: it saves time, allows division of work and reduces errors.
Special journals: Cash Book, Purchases Journal, Sales Journal, Purchases Returns Journal, Sales Returns Journal, and the Journal Proper for everything else.
Source documents: inward invoice → Purchases Journal; debit note → Purchases Returns Journal; outward invoice → Sales Journal; credit note → Sales Returns Journal.
Only credit purchases and sales of goods go into the Purchases and Sales Journals; cash transactions go into the Cash Book.

Cash books: single column; two column (cash + discount — discount allowed on the debit side, discount received on the credit side); three column (cash, bank, discount). The bank column replaces a Bank Account in the ledger.
Petty Cash Book records small expenses and saves labour.

Banking: a business usually opens a current account and gets a pass book, pay-in-slip book and cheque book. Cheques may be crossed generally or specially, endorsed to a third party, and dishonoured if the bank refuses payment.
method: Single column cash book: Dr receipts, Cr payments; balance c/d.
Cash discount appears in the discount column (two-column cash book); trade discount is never recorded.
Purchases Book: date, supplier, invoice no., details (qty × rate − trade discount + taxes/charges), amount.
mistakes: Recording cash purchases or asset purchases in the Purchases Book.
Recording trade discount in the accounts.
examples:
Examples: which book?
Goods bought on credit from Ravi → Purchases Book. Goods sold for cash → Cash Book. Goods returned to Ravi (debit note) → Purchases Returns Book. Goods returned by a customer (credit note) → Sales Returns Book. Furniture bought on credit → Journal Proper (it is not goods for resale).

Example: discounts in the cash book
100 units bought at ₹50 each less 10% trade discount → the Purchases Book records ₹4,500; the trade discount is never entered.
Ram pays ₹4,900 in full settlement of ₹5,000 → debit side of the two-column cash book: cash ₹4,900 and discount allowed ₹100.

topics.name: Journal & Ledger
topics.summary: Rare as a full question, but journal entries are needed for every numerical topic.
points: The journal is the book of original entry: transactions are recorded date-wise with a narration.
Steps in journalising: identify the accounts, classify them (personal, real, nominal), apply the rules of debit and credit, write the entry with narration.
A compound entry has more than one debit or credit; the opening entry brings forward assets and liabilities (Assets A/cs Dr, To Liabilities and Capital A/c).
The ledger groups entries by account; posting transfers each journal entry to the accounts concerned.
Balancing: a personal account's debit balance means the party owes the business (debtor); a credit balance means the business owes the party (creditor).
method: Identify accounts → classify (personal/real/nominal) → apply golden rules → write entry with narration.
mistakes: Missing narrations.
Recording trade discount.
examples:
Example: journalising a few days' transactions
1 April: started business with cash ₹50,000 → Cash A/c Dr To Capital A/c.
3 April: bought goods on credit from Mohan ₹20,000 → Purchases A/c Dr To Mohan A/c.
5 April: sold goods on credit to Sita ₹15,000 → Sita A/c Dr To Sales A/c.
10 April: paid Mohan ₹19,500 in full settlement → Mohan A/c Dr 20,000 To Cash A/c 19,500 and To Discount Received A/c 500 (a compound entry).
Ledger: Mohan's account now balances to nil; Sita's shows a debit balance of ₹15,000, so she is a debtor.
